The worst Java code I've ever seen was part of (Googles) easier mediapipe API.

They had DEEP Inheritance, manually written getters and setters which contained a few surprises (like giving back properties that already had their own getters), made intensive use of method overloading and inherited methods including methods, and these methods often took parameters that were named in a way to imply they had a certain function, only to be thrown away/used in a different way, or they were actually set, but that didn't matter as at a later point in the lifecycle these values would be overwritten before doing anything.

Trying to line up everything philosophically as classes just introduces logical issues like this. In that example, you'd probably be better off defining Person, Parent, Child, and Family classes. Since children in real life don't inherit everything evenly and directly from both parents, it doesn't make any sense to define their classes like that. Rather you should define a Person that Parent and Child will inherit from, and then you can define a Family which takes two parents and a list of children as arguments. author: @ov3rcl0cked
text:
I follow this inheritance rule in pretty much every language. Unless it's a clear cut case where inheritance makes the most sense, in terms of sharing a lot of code,  I'll opt for interfaces. I'll also prevent multiple layers of inheritance. I feel like the further you come from the base class then more confusing and implicit things can become. You end up not really knowing what the class is composed of. I instead will often look to encapsulation, and usually dependency injecting these encapsulated pieces, because it's also astonishingly easier to test. I have no strict rule around this, but I feel like if you're 5 layers of inheritance deep you're usually shooting yourself in the foot. I feel like many developers stray away from encapsulation when they can use inheritance, like one is somehow intrinsically better than the other.

A trick I've come to like when things start to get complicated with inheritance is to create an interface that defines all common methods, in C++ this would be a purely abstract class, and then have a base class for any common pieces to inherit. So in the case of a mother, father, and child, the parents might have their own base class which implements the interface, and child would just implement the interface, and maybe child could encapsulate a reference to the parents. This way any similarities in implementation the child shares with either parent is also specific to the instance of their parents. Child could even have it's own base class and you could create daughter and son, where maybe they each emphasize the characteristics of the parent who has the same sex as them, given this isn't how it actually works but serves the analogy.

I really see inheritance as mechanism to not repeat yourself, but I often see people trying to think of it too literally. Like the example mother, father, child, the child obviously literally inherits the mother and father, but you're kind of abusing the programming term "inheritance" to mean something it really doesn't. The child CLASS doesn't inherit traits from the parent CLASSES, it inherits PROPERTIES from a given INSTANCE of it's parents. Java doesn't allow multiple inheritance, and I honestly feel like that's prevented a lot of mishaps. On the other hand, I've dealt with inheritance nightmares in Pythons. I've seen a lot of people who abuse inheritance. We had a network protocol that had a major change between version 1 and 2, and the original developer implemented a base class to handle all the lower level networking pieces, many of which were common among version 1 and 2, and then inherited that into the v1 client. That's all well and good, but the real mind bender is the fact that they inherited the v1 client into the v2 client. Wild. It was so hard figuring out what happened where, and why these 2 major versions had overlapping code bases. It was a nightmare to pull that apart. This guy actually now works at Google, though I'm sure they've taught him a few lessons.

author: @kennethgee2004
text:
so that last part is to follow SOLID design.  Each class holds unique concerns, and use composition over inheritance, so that functions and responsibilities stay separated.  Inheritance has its place, but is not engineered correctly.  With classes that mainly hold data and handle some transformations inheritance is not well suited.  For objects that build upon each other like window systems, then behavioral design there says that inheritance is good.  

With all of this said it is impossible to write debt free code.  We are developers.  The use of tabs should be encouraged.  Set your editors as a preference.  We engineer differently and have unique styles.  Some solutions are only found when people can be themselves.  All of this will lead to debt though in the sees of style.  

The issue here of debt free code is not the style of coding that one uses.  The issue is how to engineer properly.  This video touched on using interfaces.  Interfaces are really important and needed in all projects.  We should be designing for interfaces as that allows for modularity.  Need a new way to access data?  Not an issue as along as the data access returns all of the correct data sets.  Which data sets are there well that is where an interface comes in, as the functions should be set based on the business logic necessary to run the front end.  In this way we can reduce debt as we are only changing one concern at a time.  Debt is not style, but failings in logic. 

I also disagree with the non-use of exceptions.  Exceptions are not just program breaks, but are failures in design, and should be looked into.  Without the exception we have no idea why the program just crashed.  What is needed is a better way to handle logging.  They will need a standard library for logging exceptions.  It is now each concerns responsibility to report the error to the logging and then handle the exception per the concern.  In the example in the video the function g handles no exceptions from H or more likely handles errors in H by raising the exception again, which passes it up to F.  This is an example of poor design.  where is the separation of concern?  if function F is the concern and functions G and H only perform data manipulation, then the responsibility for error is at function F.  if each function is its own concern, then we need a way to decouple these nested calls.

Google demonstrated a bunch of epic fails in its style guide.
A relatively simple question around tabs vs spaces should definitely be answered in favor of tabs.
The tab width of a single character MUST be different from one engineer to another because each engineer is comfortable with his/her own tab width.
What has Google achieved with its 2 spaces?
The most of engineers are uncomfortable with the view of code except those who are comfortable with 2 spaces.
In both cases the code is the same among all the engineers, but in case of 2 spaces the most of engineers are uncomfortable with the code.
What a great accomplishment!
Google does not use exceptions and this is an extremely dramatic fail in its style guide.
Imagine a situation when a variable of some class is created, a constructor of that class is called and it finds out during construction that the object cannot be constructed.
For example, because of a temporary lack of resources needed for the construction.
How could I find out that the variable cannot be used then in the code after its definition, because it is not constructed completely?
The only way a constructor can notify the code after the variable definition that the variable has not been constructed is to throw an exception.
Another situation: imagine I use a custom allocator for std::vector.
How can the allocator notify the code working with a std::vector object that the space for more elements cannot be allocated?
And finally, perhaps you will be laughing but the standard library throws exceptions too.
So what?
Not to use the standard library?
Really?
Try to find a fail that is more epic than that of Google in its design of not to use exceptions at all in their style guide.
That is why they even made an attempt to return to using exceptions but it is already too-too late and therefore they have failed even with that...

The list of things you picked from the style guide is weird, your also not critical of any of these.

* spaces-vs-tabs is a meaningless debate things display differently in editors based on font and many other things, also there are many cases where displaying things different is desired with spaces this is not possible.

Also single return path isn't the reason for no exceptions, with C++ and RAII single return path is no longer a thing which most people recommend, in fact it's sometimes nicer to have multiple return paths (within reason)

Instead a child has-a mother and has-a father in which case mother and father would be members of the child, you also completely switch the example to a car after so not showing an actual alternative. I don't get the "bad inheritance" example. A child would NEVER inherit from either Mother nor Father, and it will EVEN NEVER-ER inheritj from BOTH

Inheritance models a "Is a" relationship. In your example you didn't seem to be aware of that basic principle about inheritance. But the example you gave implied that a child IS a Mother AND a Father which makes little sense regardless of coding style

But then if you KNOW you will need to add features that apply to EVERY person (Maybe for this particular program every person should breath, and implementing that though composition of a "Lungs" object is kinda convoluted, instead you implement a Breath method directly in Person that calls itself every so often so that the person stays alive), THEN you could get away with some implementation inheritance. Since the moment a person that does NOT breath appears (For example a fish person, that would be killed by breathing air). Then you would have to do a lot of code rewriting. Since if you mindless let FishPerson inherit from Person. You might not even realize why all your Fish Persons are dead on arrival (A problem that would have not happened with composition. Since you would immediately realize that you should NOT give them regular Lungs, but instead some sort of "Water Lungs". Composition + Interface Inheritance is more redundant. A better example would've been to say that Child inherits from Person, but since a Mother is also someone's Child, the multiple inheritance scenario would be Mother inheriting both from Person and Child. author: @mathgeniuszach
text:
I've always heard terrible explanations as to why "inheritance is bad", and yours is... well it's better than the rest, but you still make the mistake in the diamond problem of extending two classes where it doesn't make sense to, i.e. a child is not both their father and mother, they have a father and mother, thus this is a bad example and composition would be clearly used. These bad examples were one of the reasons I never took these "arguments" seriously.

A better example is when modularity is involved. Say you want to create an object that is both a Sprite (has x and y coordinates and can be drawn), and is a Damagable (has hp and stats). Perhaps you may even want to change stats based on position and so interactions between both are necessary; changing one should change the other. Both of these make sense to have internal state to potentially inherit from. However, the diamond problem occurs here too.

There are still drawbacks to composition, like desynced state between child members. I always say to use what makes sense, don't pick something because you always did it that way.

author: @triularity
text:
If C++ developers just assume exceptions could be thrown by almost everything, and defensively code for that, then dealing with them generally isn't a problem. Of course, this is easier when done in a language which has them from the start (e.g. java), rather than after the fact. To help mitigate the problems, there is always the noexcept declaration (but only if using C++11 or later).. and even its design is broken since it doesn't prevent them indirectly bubbling up and pulling the rug out from the function. I think it would have been better for the compiler to require the function dealt with any potential exception to guarantee nothing (like you would with checked exceptions in java).

[For the record, I avoid using C++, unless I have too -- it's basically a dumpster fire of things piled on top of things, piled on top of things, over the decades and many revisions. With a new spec seemingly every year now, it's only getting worse (no mature language should be changing that often)]

author: @dabbinchap
text: Not using exceptions is not viable with containers using dynamic memory. Constructors, copy constructors and copy assignment operators MUST be able to throw if they cannot allocate enough memory. And since they must throw, you must catch the exception. Sure, you could ban allocating memory in constructors, and force use of separate reserve methods. Sure, you could ban the use of copy constructors/assignment, but how the hell would you make a copy of an object that owns dynamic memory? Maybe use a obj.copy(T& to) function, which makes a copy from object to argument reference and returns true or false depending on whether the copy succeeded. That only works as long as programmers remember to explicitly delete copy constructor and assignment methods for a type; if they don't some other programmers will certainly do an implicit copy and then all hell breaks loose. Deleting copy methods plus overloading some global copy function (with boolean return value) is messy. Using such semantics is messy. In these cases just using exceptions works best.

author: @bushrat0118
text:
Ok I understand the "You should learn C first because it teaches you how a computer works" argument is really common, and I used to believe it as well. But now I actually think this is a bad take. Despite what everyone thinks their start in programming was, nobody started writing in C.

My grandfather's generation learnt by writing ladder diagrams, a trivial language with arbitrary rules and little bearing on the fundamental hardware.

My dad's generation learnt by writing in BASIC, a trivial language with arbitrary rules and little bearing on the fundamental hardware.

My generation learnt with JavaScript, a trivial language with arbitrary rules and little bearing on the fundamental hardware.

Sure, in a computer science course at the university level you'll learn something like C right now, but does C really teach you how a computer "works"? It completely obfuscates how registers, caching, context switching, etc. work. C only feels bare metal because you already know how a computer works and you're projecting over the gaps.

By the logic of "learning how a computer really works", you could make the argument that people should be writing assembly as their first language, and some schools still believe that. The problem is, assembly is awful for teaching how to think algorithmically. 

This is why most schools would teach maths and assembly: something high level for algorithms, and something low level for implementation.

Now, we're in a world where languages are expressive enough, and computers are fast enough, that you can write complex algorithms in a very expressive language and compile them down to fundamental instructions.

The C memory model is no less arbitrary than the Rust model. 

After all of that, I still think you should learn C, but not because you need it to understand a computer. You should learn C for the same reason you should learn Zig, Rust, TypeScript, BASIC, etc., Because knowledge is transferrable, and learning anything helps with understanding everything.

author: @Diablokiller999
text:
When people ask me, how they should learn programming, I ALWAYS say - buy an Arduino learn kit for $20, do some projects with it, remove the Arduino Bootloader, do the same projects again without Arduino header and alter this code to use pointers.
After that, you've got a pretty good understand on how C works, how compiler work, how RAM and storage devices work and how processors work.
Next step would be to grab a Raspberry Pi and program a driver or two for the ICs from your Arduino kit and you know basically everything there is to know for a starting programmer.
You know C (and can switch to C++), you know hardware, you know drivers, you know how to extend the most used operating system in the world.
Taking interpreter languages like Python or going wild with web development could be your next step, easy to learn an master if you've got the basics from C.
All the code you will ever write, runs on computers so its one of the most valuable things to know how they work, either for optimization, portability and to know in general what the heck you are even doing.
Also it's getting hard to find embedded programmers these days, since it seems (to me) that no one wants to go through all the hustle with computer knowledge.

author: @Tapajara
text: I started to outgrow C in the mid 1980's. Most new programming languages grew in the wrong directions. They threw out things I wanted to keep (e.g. pointers) and adopted things I didn't want (e.g. garbage collection). So Rust is immediately disqualified. None of them adopted Unicode as their base character set, although Python did a mediocre job in this area. You'd never want to write an operating system with that crippled interpretive scripting language. In 1988 I started developing what I now call ϕPPL. The 'ϕ' in its name emphasizes that its base character set is Unicode. PPL stands for "Parallel Programming Language". ϕ is the mathematical phi (rhymes with pie) that was brought into Unicode with the ANSI extensions. There is another φ that is part of the Greek Alphabet and you can pronounce it like "fee" if you want to say it that way. My entire tool chain is written in C and assembly. That speaks for itself.

author: @alpheusmadsen8485
text:
I am amazed at how easy it is to learn languages like Common Lisp and Forth -- at their core, they are *very* simple!  (Lispers might "pshaw" that statement -- Common Lisp is simple?  But what about Scheme?  But I die on this hill:  Common Lisp has a simple core, and then specifies a lot of beautiful things Scheme "offloads" into libraries, but are needed or at least greatly desired to get anything useful done!)

In any case, the languages may be simple, but because they are so powerful, people try to do things that are pretty much impossible in other languages -- and I am convinced that people think these languages are hard to understand because they can't disentangle the difficult problems from the languages themselves!

But Haskell is complex.  I have a quantum love-hate relationship with it -- I simultaneously love and hate the language at the same time, and I love and hate all its features all the way down to its fundamentals.  As a mathematician, I am impressed with its mathematical purity, but I can't help but think "You shouldn't have to have a PhD in math to program a computer!"

text: Get a bunch of datasheets online and learn to understand flight times in devices like logic, programmable logic, common microcontrollers, and overview of the interfaces/buses your code is working with. author: @SidewaysCytlan
text:
No no no. I learned how to program in Actionscript (yes, you can laugh), but what *really* kickstarted my programming career was when I learned 6502 assembly. To this date, I think learning 6502 assembly (or a similar 70-80s microprocessor) is *the* best way to learn how computers *really* work. It puts you into this small little sandbox, but gives you the tools you need from grown-up architectures. 6502 assembly has pointers. And it can dereference pointers. And it gives you that in a memory space that's only 64K. Even if you mess up, you can still debug and follow along where your pointer went and how it got there. C isn't "low level", 6502 assembly is low level and an amazing tool for when you get around to actually learning C and modern computing.
Mind you, I'm not a greybeard. The 6502 was outdated and obsolete before I even was born. It's still an amazing low-level architecture that you can expand on when you dive into x86(/-64) or ARM, or any other architecture that's still at the forefront of computing technology today.

author: @neilbradley
text:
Been in the industry about 37 years now, and I've noticed a trend of graduates getting considerably worse over time. The downward slide. I blame the schools for chasing. I have personally witnessed:

* A Stanford CS graduate who had never seen and did not know what assembly language is (he was shocked when his code crashed down inside modules that didn't have source and didn't know what he was looking at)
* A master's degree holder in CS who didn't know it was a bad idea to hand a sorted list to quicksort
* A younger engineer not understanding that simply wrapping a kernel call in a coroutine won't make it nonblocking
* Another who didn't know what swap or virtual memory was
* A prevalent "don't know/don't want to know" attitude about everything

I've seen so much lousy C++ or "object oriented" code where people are going through the motions without any understanding of why or what they're doing.
